snippet.title: Best KASOL Food Walk l Hemp Coffee + Hummus + Shakshuka + Falafel King + German Bakery + Shambu Momo
snippet.description:
Join us on a vibrant food walk through Kasol as we explore some of the most loved cafes and hidden gems in the area. Hosted by Anubhav Sapra and Khushboo Barry, this trail is packed with stories, flavours, and memorable conversations.

We began at The Evergreen on Manikaran Road near the Forest Rest House, where we met Jatin Sharma and Tal Gross. Their combo crispy chicken platter was a mountain feast layered with bold Middle Eastern flavours-crispy schnitzel, creamy labneh, comforting shakshuka, fresh salad, French fries, and warm naan, all brought together with a drizzle of tahini and chilli garlic sauce. Hearty, wholesome, and deeply satisfying.

Next stop was King Falafel near Nature Park. Their signature falafel, paired with hummus, tahini, laffa, and fries, was a pocket-sized powerhouse of texture and taste-crunchy, fluffy, spiced, and truly heart warming.

At Little Italy Inn on Manikaran Road, we met Vanita and tried their farmhouse pizza loaded with fresh toppings and gooey cheese, followed by a balanced, creamy tiramisu. We also spoke to the young owner, who shared how her parents started the cafe, turning it into a beloved spot over the years.

We dropped by Offlimits Cafe, India’s first hemp cafe, where we met one of the young co-founders, Mayank. Hemp is native to this region, and that’s what inspired them to reimagine it in the culinary space. This unique cafe blends locally sourced produce with hemp-based ingredients in a contemporary setting. It’s a refreshing, offbeat stop for anyone looking to explore alternative, mindful food options.

At German Bakery, Balram treated us to a soft, flaky croissant and a decadent cream cheesecake. We chatted about the legacy of German bakery their evolution across India, and how each carries a unique local story while maintaining their classic charm.

In Nature Park, Shambhu Momo served us piping hot chicken momos, thanks to Sunil. Juicy, flavour-packed, and just the kind of snack you crave in the chilly mountain breeze.

Moon Dance Cafe, near the bridge, was another memorable stop. Their red and white sauce pastas were comforting, the trout fresh from local streams, and the biryani rich with warm spices. We later returned to try their spaghetti pasta - light, flavourful, and indulgent. With its laid-back vibe, artistic interiors, and garden seating, Moon Dance is a soulful cafe that invites you to linger.

This food trail through Kasol is more than just meals, it’s a journey across forest trails, cozy cafes, warm kitchens, and a melting pot of global and local tastes. Watch the full episode to soak it all in.

Moon Dance Cafe, near the bridge, was another memorable stop. Their red and white sauce pastas were comforting, the trout fresh from local streams, and the biryani rich with warm spices. We later returned to try their spaghetti pasta - light, flavourful, and indulgent. With its laid-back vibe, artistic interiors, and garden seating, Moon Dance is a soulful cafe that invites you to linger.

This food trail through Kasol is more than just meals, it’s a journey across forest trails, cozy cafes, warm kitchens, and a melting pot of global and local tastes. Watch the full episode to soak it all in.

snippet.title: Art of making Street Style Tomato Soup in Delhi🍜🥣😍 Massive making of Real Tomato Healthy Soup🍅🍅
snippet.description:
Welcome back to the channel, food lovers! In this video, we take you on a flavorful journey to the streets of Delhi, where a street vendor showcases the art of making real, healthy, street-style tomato soup in MASSIVE quantities! 🍜

Delhi winters and a hot cup of tomato soup go hand in hand, and nothing beats the rich, tangy, spicy, and buttery street version made live on a big tawa with love and flair. This is not just soup; it's a warm hug in a bowl! 😍

Watch as bhaiya starts with fresh, juicy tomatoes that are pressure cooked until soft. Then comes the exciting part – blending the boiled tomatoes into a rich pulp, which is then poured into a hot, butter-laden pan. Spices like black pepper, salt, red chilli powder, chaat masala, and secret masalas are added to give that authentic desi tang. A dash of sugar balances the acidity while cornflour slurry gives it that smooth, thick consistency. 🥄

To finish it off, bhaiya adds cubes of butter, a generous handful of chopped coriander, and crunchy croutons for texture. The aroma that fills the air is absolutely divine – a blend of tomato richness and street-style spice that warms your soul instantly. This is what real Delhi-style tomato soup is all about – wholesome, healthy, spicy, and full of love. ❤️

If you enjoy watching authentic Indian street food preparation, this video will keep you hooked from start to finish. Perfect for soup lovers, foodies, and anyone who wants to relive the taste of Delhi’s winter evenings.

snippet.title: Ep - 14, Delhi’s Best DAL @ Sialkot Dhaba + Gabbar/Gabbi Kadi Chawal l Multani Moth Kachori + Chaap
snippet.description:
We went on a street food tour in Geeta Colony with our host Rishabh Bhatia, a young man who knows the food scene of East Delhi like the back of his hand. With a friendly smile and a clear passion for the local food culture, he walked us through lanes lined with food joints that have stood the test of time and tastes.

Our first stop was Gabbar Kadhi Chawal, a small outlet with a quirky name that serves up what might just be one of the best plates of rajma kadhi chawal in the city. You can go for either rajma chawal, kadhi chawal, or a mix of both. We chose the mix and were greeted with thick, flavorful curries poured over rice—simple, hearty, and deeply satisfying.

Next, we made our way to Nagpal Di Hatti for their quintessential Multani moth kachori. Here, khasta moong dal kachoris are served with thick moth ki dal, mixed with a special spice blend and chutneys, and topped with a small amount of rice. The magic lies in the Multani masala that elevates the dish with its bold and earthy punch. Rishabh showed us how he enjoys it best—by crushing the kachoris into the dal, letting the flavors meld into one soul-satisfying bowl.

At Yellow Bowl, we were greeted with a menu full of playful names and wild combinations. Known for their variety of chaap and momos, we picked their Naughty Momo, Cheese Corn Momo, and Punjabi Chaap after a fun chat with the owner. It was a youthful, experimental spot with food that matched its energy—bold, cheesy, and crowd-pleasing.

We took a breather at a cozy little cafe called Piyega The Coffee Co. It’s a snug hideout offering a mix of classic and fusion coffees. We tried their Irish Blonde and Italiana Tiramisu, both served in stylish cups, balancing strong coffee notes with sweet, dessert-like tones.

Our next stop was Ramesh Vaishno Dhaba, a place that celebrates East Delhi’s deep love for chaap. The variety here was astounding, and the aroma coming from their butter-laden dishes was irresistible. On Rishabh’s recommendation, we tried the stuffed chaap, pudina chaap, tawa chaap, and a fantastic pyaaz roti. The stuffed chaap, dunked in butter, was the bestseller for a reason—rich, spicy, and absolutely addictive. The pyaaz roti, packed with generous bits of onion and baked in a tandoor, was a great companion to the chaap.

One of the most heartfelt stops was Pyarelal Sialkot Vegetarian. This place has been part of Rishabh’s childhood, and he recalled fondly how the owner would always hand out candies to kids, a gesture of warmth that stayed with him over the years. We sat down to try their slow-cooked dal makhani and paneer lababdar with rotis. The dal, cooked for around nine hours, was creamy, luxurious, and comforting—truly a dish that felt like a hug.

We ended the tour at Gogia Shudh Khoya & Paneer Bhandar with something sweet. Here, we tried their jalebi, rabri, and kulhad doodh. The jalebis were crisp and syrupy, the rabri was thick and luscious, and the kulhad doodh had that smoky, earthy flavor that only clay cups can lend. It was the perfect ending to a walk that was not just about food, but memories, stories, and the unmistakable warmth of Delhi’s streets.

Every member of the Gokuldham community looks everywhere for water, but they are all unsuccessful.  Champaklal ultimately chastises Iyer for continuing to find water in various locations.  To solve the water problem, everyone in the community is depending on the alternatives.  To find out that the water will arrive the following morning, Bhide, Sodhi, and Popatlal visit the municipality water supply in the interim.  People in the community are eager to order a water tanker after receiving false optimism from the municipality's water supply, but Champaklal is against it.  Now what are they going to do?

About The Show:
----------------------------
Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah is a comedy show inspired by the famous humorous column 'Duniya Ne Undha Chashmah' written by the eminent Gujarati writer Mr. Tarak Mehta. This show revolves around the Gada Family which consists of uneducated businessmen Jethalal Champaklal Gada, Jethalal’s Wife Daya & their naughty Son Tipendra Gada living in 'Gokuldham Co-operative Society' and covers topical issues which are socially relevant. In case of a problem and emergency, Jethalal Gada often rushes to Taarak Mehta to seek his help and guidance as he finds a philosopher in him. The residents of the housing society, help each other find solutions when they face common, real-life challenges and get involved in sticky situations.
